topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the World Through Different Eyes
target_audience: University students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

outline.topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the World Through Different Eyes
outline.target_audience: University students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

sections.title: The Perspective Problem: Two Maps, One Forest
sections.content: Introduce the concept that coordinates are not absolute; they depend on the 'basis' or perspective chosen. We begin with a scenario where two characters describe the same location differently.
sections.example: A Human uses a standard North-East grid (Standard Basis), while an Owl perched on a tilted branch uses the direction of the branch and its perpendicular as her grid. A mouse at point (3,2) for the Human is at a completely different coordinate for the Owl.

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: What is a Basis?
sections.content: Briefly define a basis as a set of linearly independent vectors that span the space. Visually represent the 'Standard Basis' (i, j) as a rigid square grid.
sections.example: Show the vector v = 2i + 3j. Explain that the numbers (2, 3) are just 'instructions' (2 steps right, 3 steps up) relative to the grid lines.

sections.title: The 'Dictionary': The Transition Matrix
sections.content: Explain that to translate between the Human and the Owl, we need a 'dictionary.' This dictionary is the Transition Matrix (P). It is built by expressing the Owl's basis vectors in terms of the Human's coordinates.
sections.example: If the Owl's first unit vector looks like (1, 1) to the Human and her second looks like (-1, 1), these vectors become the columns of our Transition Matrix P.

sections.title: The Mathematical Transformation
sections.content: Introduce the formula: [x]basis_A = P * [x]basis_B. Show how multiplying the Owl's coordinates by the matrix 'warps' her tilted grid back into the Human's standard grid.
sections.example: Animate the Owl's tilted grid lines stretching and rotating until they align with the Human's square grid. If the Owl sees a point at (1, 1), the matrix multiplication reveals the Human sees it at (0, 2).

sections.title: The Inverse Journey: Going Back
sections.content: Discuss how to go from the Standard Basis to the New Basis using the inverse matrix (P⁻¹). This emphasizes that change of basis is a two-way street.
sections.example: The Human wants to tell the Owl where a tasty snack is. He takes his coordinates, applies the inverse matrix P⁻¹, and gives the Owl instructions that match her tilted world.

sections.title: Summary and Real-World Utility
sections.content: Recap the core idea: Change of basis doesn't move the point; it just changes the language we use to describe its location. Mention applications like image compression (JPEG) or facial recognition (Eigenfaces).
sections.example: In computer graphics, a character's arm has its own basis. When the arm moves, we change the basis to relate the 'hand coordinates' back to the 'body coordinates' to render the image correctly.

storyboard.title: The Perspective Problem: Two Maps, One Forest
lecture_lines: Coordinates depend on your chosen perspective or basis.
Meet the Human, using a standard North-East grid.
Meet the Owl, using her tilted branch as reference.
A mouse's location looks different to each observer.
Same physical point, but two different sets of coordinates.
animations: Show a standard grid (Human) and a tilted grid (Owl) overlapping in the center.
Place a mouse icon at (3, 2) on the standard grid and label it '(3, 2)' in #00FF00.
Flash the Human's unit vectors in #0000FF to highlight the standard basis.
Flash the Owl's tilted unit vectors in #FFFF00 to highlight the alternate basis.
Scale the mouse icon and display 'One Point, Two Descriptions' in #FFFFFF.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Check: What is a Basis?
lecture_lines: A basis is a set of independent spanning vectors.
The standard basis uses unit vectors i and j.
This creates a familiar, rigid square grid.
Vector v is just instructions relative to this grid.
Change the basis, and you change the instructions.
animations: Show the standard basis vectors i in #FF0000 and j in #00FF00 with labels.
Draw vector v = 2i + 3j from the origin and label it 'v = [2, 3]^T' in #FFFFFF.
Animate 2 steps along i then 3 steps along j to illustrate the coordinates.

storyboard.title: The 'Dictionary': The Transition Matrix
lecture_lines: A transition matrix translates between different bases.
Describe the Owl's basis vectors using Human coordinates.
These Human-relative vectors become the matrix columns.
Each column translates one basis vector's language.
This matrix acts as our mathematical dictionary.
animations: Display Owl's basis vectors b1=(1,1) and b2=(-1,1) in #FFFF00 on the standard grid.
Animate the vector coordinates (1,1) and (-1,1) moving into a 2x2 matrix bracket.
Label the matrix 'P - Transition Matrix' in #00FFFF.
Highlight the first column of P in #FF8800 and the second column in #FF00FF.
Flash the Owl's basis vectors again to emphasize they are the columns of P.

storyboard.title: The Mathematical Transformation
lecture_lines: Multiply the matrix to convert coordinates between bases.
Tilted grid lines align with the standard square grid.
The transformation reveals how the other person sees it.
animations: Display the formula '[x]_Human = P * [x]_Owl' at the top in #FFFFFF.
Show the Owl's tilted grid in #FFFF00 across the screen.
Animate the tilted grid transforming/unwarping into the standard square grid.
Plot a point at (1,1) in Owl's coordinates and show it transition to (0,2) in Human's coordinates.
Highlight the final coordinates (0,2) in #00FF00.

storyboard.title: The Inverse Journey: Going Back
lecture_lines: Use the inverse matrix to return to the original basis.
Change of basis is a two-way mathematical street.
The Human translates his coordinates for the Owl's world.
animations: Display the inverse formula '[x]_Owl = P^-1 * [x]_Human' in #FFFFFF.
Show a static point on the standard grid and highlight its coordinates.
Animate the standard grid warping into the Owl's tilted grid #FFFF00.

storyboard.title: Summary and Real-World Utility
lecture_lines: Changing the basis doesn't move the physical point.
It simply changes the language used to describe location.
Essential for JPEG compression and computer graphics.
animations: Show a point labeled 'Fixed Location' with two sets of coordinates updating simultaneously.
Display 'Image Compression' and 'Computer Graphics' in #00FFFF with simple icons.
Fade out all elements and show 'Same Vector, Different Basis' in #FFFFFF.
